title: Better for everyone, worse overall?
hook: A treatment wins for small stones and for large ones. Can it still lose overall?

doesNotKnow: why group sizes change an overall rate

misconception: If A beats B in every subgroup, A must beat B overall.
objective: The learner can explain that an overall rate is an average of subgroup rates weighted by subgroup size, so a treatment that gets most of the hard cases can win in every subgroup and still lose overall.

claims.text: In the kidney-stone data, treatment A cured 81 of 87 small-stone patients and 192 of 263 large-stone patients; treatment B cured 234 of 270 small-stone and 55 of 80 large-stone patients.
claims.source: C. R. Charig, D. R. Webb, S. R. Payne and J. E. Wickham (1986), 'Comparison of treatment of renal calculi by open surgery, percutaneous nephrolithotomy, and extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy', BMJ 292: 879-882; as presented in S. A. Julious and M. A. Mullee (1994), 'Confounding and Simpson's paradox', BMJ 309: 1480.

claims.text: Those counts give A 93% (small) and 73% (large) against B's 87% and 69%, but overall A 78.0% (273/350) and B 82.6% (289/350).
263 of A's 350 patients had large stones, against 80 of B's 350, and both treatments did worse on large stones.
claims.source: From the counts in c1: A large 263/350; B large 80/350; each treatment's large-stone rate is below its small-stone rate.

claims.text: An overall rate is the average of the subgroup rates weighted by the share of patients in each subgroup.
claims.source: (wins_small + wins_large)/(n_small + n_large) = (n_small/n) x rate_small + (n_large/n) x rate_large.

claims.text: Keeping each treatment's subgroup rates fixed and 350 patients per treatment, giving A 220 or fewer of the 343 large-stone patients makes A's overall rate higher than B's.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/better-in-every-group-worse-overall/model.ts arms(k): A overall = ((350-k) x 81/87 + k x 192/263)/350; B overall = ((7+k) x 234/270 + (343-k) x 55/80)/350. Re-run: A ahead for k <= 220, B ahead for k >= 221; at an even split (k = 171) A 83.3% vs B 77.9%. Off the real split, cured counts are expected values, not whole people.

claims.text: In the 1986 study, A was open surgery and B was percutaneous nephrolithotomy (keyhole surgery).
claims.source: Charig et al. (1986), BMJ 292: 879-882; Julious and Mullee (1994), BMJ 309: 1480, Table 1.

recall.question: School X has a higher pass rate than school Y among rich pupils and among poor pupils. Can Y still have the higher pass rate overall?
options: Yes, if Y has many more rich pupils
Only if the schools are the same size
recall.why: An overall rate weights each group by its size. If rich pupils pass more and Y is mostly rich pupils, Y's average leans on its easiest group.
